name: Satellite Imagery
title: Satellite Imagery
answer: Satellite imagery as alternative data covers optical, radar, and thermal observations of the Earth's surface collected by public and commercial constellations. It is used to infer activity that is hard to see from ground reports, such as construction progress, crop health, shipping traffic, and industrial output. The data is not just the image, it includes metadata like capture time, location, and sensor type. For an economist, it is a high-frequency, geographically precise signal that can be paired with traditional statistics.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Satellite imagery as alternative data covers optical, radar, and thermal observations of the Earth's surface collected by public and commercial constellations. It is used to infer activity that is hard to see from ground reports, such as construction progress, crop health, shipping traffic, and industrial output. The data is not just the image, it includes metadata like capture time, location, and sensor type. For an economist, it is a high-frequency, geographically precise signal that can be paired with traditional statistics.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work runs on a pipeline that ingests raw scenes from satellite downlinks, often through cloud storage and APIs. Processing requires compute for orthorectification, atmospheric correction, and cloud masking, typically on GPU or distributed CPU clusters. Storage is large because each scene is hundreds of megabytes and revisit rates can be daily. Analysts access the data through geospatial libraries and cloud platforms rather than downloading everything locally.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The method starts with defining an area and time window, then selecting scenes with acceptable cloud cover and resolution. Analysts build features from pixel values, such as vegetation indices or changes in built-up area, and may train models to detect objects like ships, trucks, or storage tanks. Validation uses ground truth from permits, port logs, or field surveys. The output is often a time series that can be compared with economic indicators.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk center on licensing, privacy, and national security. Commercial imagery has terms of use that restrict redistribution, and some governments limit access to certain resolutions or locations. Privacy concerns arise when imagery captures individuals or sensitive sites, even if taken from orbit. Provenance matters because a model's output is only as reliable as the sensor calibration and processing chain behind it. This site tracks 219 compliance and regulation pages, and satellite imagery sits within that broader regulatory map.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The field is moving toward more frequent revisits, cheaper small satellites, and automated analysis that turns raw pixels into ready-to-use indicators. Fusion with other alternative data, such as shipping records or mobile location, is likely to grow. Regulatory attention on remote sensing and data privacy may shape what can be collected and shared. For the AI Economist, the value will come from linking these physical signals to financial and economic outcomes.
